segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You appreciate, Jacques, this is quite extraordinary information, because here we have a situation where the person who's known by the pseudonym Gilbert, who you know personally and from whom you have corroborative documentation asserting this exchange with a non-human entity — this is somebody who's allegedly had direct communication with a non-human entity in a presumably US government, or maybe private aerospace, facility, at the behest of the US government, in a non-classified way, which is extraordinary in itself. Is what Gilbert learned one of the reasons why you now say the phenomenon operates from what you call higher reality levels, reprocessing human consciousness?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: No. That has been, to me, one of the most valid hypotheses for the last 50 years. And there was considerable work done in France especially, but also in other parts of Europe and in the USSR, on the subject, and that work, when we review it now, is consistent with that idea: that this is at a different level.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Jacques, one of the things I love about you is that you do your level best to honor your obligations to people like Gilbert, not to reveal too much about confidential things. You're like a journalist, you're protecting your sources. One of the questions I'd love to ask you directly is: you've spent your whole adult life investigating the whole phenomenon of UFOs, UAPs. Do you feel now, at 86 years old, with your final book, that you now know the answer?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: In science, it's a valid question, of course. I know some answers, and, as always in science, they suggest other questions. You discover that what you thought was a little cloud of dust somewhere is the Andromeda nebula and it's outside your own galaxy — well, that opens up a hundred new questions that you had never thought about before. So science works by expanding the range of the unknown. Things are more and more unknown as science progresses. It's not our knowledge that increases, but the range of unknown things. Look at medicine today: when I talk to Dr. Garry Nolan at Stanford, he says never mind the genome, the genome, we're going to work on that for the next 20 years, but there are all these other levels of other entities, and now we have no idea where the computers are going to come from that will enable us even to enter the data.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Let's come at it from this angle, though, Jacques. If you can't tell me the answer, what's the one question that you still cannot answer after all these years of investigating? What's the one vexing question in the UAP field that Dr. Jacques Vallée still cannot answer?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Well, the main question. There has been no disclosure. We've known since the 1950s that these things were real, that they were material when they came here, that they emerged out of nowhere — they don't come through space, they come from time-space, and they come very likely from a knowledge of other dimensions. Now, if you talk to physicists today, they'll say there's nothing new there, you teach about other dimensions in physics today. The question is how would we get there, what does it really mean for us in our universe?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I remember, my first job was in Texas, and part of my work was working on the map of the planet Mars for NASA. The other job was taking spectra of faraway galaxies north of El Paso, at McDonald Observatory, where you spend four hours at the prime focus of the big telescope — you drive it like a truck to get the data. As I was going home at dawn, you close the dome and you go home, I was with my boss, Dr. Gérard de Vaucouleurs, and we had the whole Texas sky above us. And I said: what do you think, is this all expanding? He said yes, the best theory — this was in the mid-1960s — the best theory is the expansion, because of the spectrum. It could be challenged, but that's the best theory we have. But that means we're in a bubble that's expanding, and I think they will find that there are other bubbles, and the best model of the universe is: you go to your kitchen and you fill the kitchen sink with warm water and you pour detergent until you've got bubbles all over the place. Some bubbles will contract and some bubbles will expand. He said that's what I think they will find the universe is. Remember, we were responsible for the catalog of galaxies. We had data that galaxies were aligned along thresholds of things, and now that has been developed in major ways, particularly in France, and with the new telescope that's now operating. That will decide it. But this is where these objects could be coming from.
